divergence: the password was never invented — everything runs on the honor system and a guard named Doug
story_angle: deadpan report of a catastrophe that everyone involved considers a great success
headline: Pentagon Hails 2.3 Million Guestbook Sign-Ins as 'Model of Efficient Oversight'
deck: Nation's Data Breach Transformed into Bureaucratic Triumph with One Man and a Clipboard.
article:
In an unprecedented turn of events, the Pentagon has officially declared the unauthorized duplication of 2.3 million sensitive files a shining example of efficient oversight, thanks in large part to the exceptional diligence of Doug, the sole security guard overseeing the national data center. Doug's single clipboard captured 47,000 sign-ins before lunch, with zero refusals, as intruders seemingly embraced the honor system with gusto, proving that accountability can be as simple as a well-placed ledger.

Officials are praising the initiative, as each copied file now carries the esteemed 'honorably reviewed' stamp, elevating the magnitude of data loss to a glorious form of bureaucratic accomplishment. Accompanying this assessment, Deputy Undersecretary for Administrative Excellence, Margaret Hightower, stated, "True efficiency is knowing how to embrace an unintentional mass access event as a managed and contained affair. We’ve effectively turned chaos into paperwork."

In response to the incident, the county DMV has rolled out urgent new guidance for commuters, recommending the addition of 'visiting' to their daily ledgers to ensure compliance in light of Doug’s continued success. As one DMV employee quipped, “Why bother with IDs when you can simply drop your name in a book? It’s practically community service."

Citizens now queue with pens ready while Doug, still at his post, logs every arrival without pause.
author: Mabel Hargrove, Senior Ledger Correspondent

oped.title: Clipboards Over Chaos: Why Doug's Guestbook Saves Us All
oped.author: Lord Percival Snodgrass, Baronet of Unassailable Logic and Curator of the Museum of My Own Opinions
oped.body: The Pentagon deserves praise, not scorn, for transforming that minor data mishap into a triumph of one clipboard and Doug's watchful eye. Critics claim 2.3 million sign-ins signals failure, yet this ignores how the honor system rewards the virtuous—such as myself, who always prints legibly and offers Doug a mint. The real culprits are those sloppy signers whose hats blocked Doug's view, forcing him to squint. Passwords would only encourage laziness; instead, we need mandatory guestbooks at every ATM and voting booth, with my personal veto power over anyone who scrawls too hastily. Doug once waved me through without signing, proving the system's flexibility for the deserving. Expand this nationwide, and perhaps Doug will finally notice my superior penmanship over those hat-wearing ingrates.

classifieds.text: Help Wanted: Pentagon guard Doug urgently needs 12 backup clipboard monitors for 2.3M daily sign-ins. Must promise not to sell the guestbook on the honor-system dark web.
For Sale: 47 servers full of 'secure' files now publicly signed by 2.3M guests. Doug says take them, he’s tired of the line at the door.
Lost & Found: One nation’s entire data integrity, last seen in the Pentagon lobby guestbook. Return to Doug for a heartfelt thank-you and a smiley face stamp.
Personals: To the 2.3M who signed my clipboard yesterday—sorry your secrets are now public. Coffee on me if you promise not to sue Doug.

panels.caption: Pentagon chief: "Doug logged 2.3 million sign-ins on that clipboard. Efficiency defined."
Doug, to a passing colonel: "Yeah, half signed as 'Kim from Pyongyang'—honor system's working great."
Chief, beaming: "Zero breaches!" Doug hands the last file box to a smiling stranger in a trench coat.

stories.headline: Silicon Valley Firms Contract Clipboard Services After Pentagon Model Gains Traction
stories.deck: Venture rounds now allocate separate line for on-site honor overseers
stories.article:
Several cloud storage companies have begun placing one guard named Doug at each server rack entrance, requiring every employee to print their name and stated task on a bound ledger before retrieving files. The change followed internal memos citing the Pentagon's 2.3 million sign-ins as proof that visible accountability reduces accidental data exposure.

Procurement records show contracts awarded to a new firm supplying identical clipboards and ballpoint pens, with one Austin startup reporting a 40 percent decline in employees accessing records outside their listed department. Doug Ramirez, stationed at a data center in San Jose, confirmed no one has refused to sign since the policy took effect.
